Bilayer magnetic composites combine random anisotropy hexaferrite nanocomposites and soft metallic magnetic materials in a dielectric matrix.
Reflection loss (RL) increased from 25 dB (single MW layer) up to 35 dB with bilayer structures.
Absorption bandwidth increased by up to 20% with the addition of a second layer.
The absorption frequency can be tuned by adjusting the thickness of the second layer, shifting by about 1 GHz.
Optimal absorption occurs at specific thicknesses; too thin or too thick layers reduce effectiveness.
Soft magnetic composite (SMC) layers with phosphate insulating shells prevent eddy currents and maintain high permeability at higher frequencies.
Amorphous magnetic microwires have an iron core and glass coating, with 12 µm core diameter and 1 mm length.
Hexaferrite powders were synthesized by co-precipitation followed by calcination at 900°C.
The dielectric matrix used was Titan’s Unilak white water-based enamel for powders and Hempel’s primer undercoat for microwires.
Reflection loss measurements were performed in an anechoic chamber using horn antennas and a network analyzer from 0.5 to 18 GHz.
Bilayer theory equations relate reflection loss to permittivity, permeability, and thickness of each layer, requiring impedance matching for optimal absorption.
Random anisotropy magnets consist of nanocrystallites with randomly oriented anisotropy axes, enhancing broadband absorption.
Cu and Mn doping in hexaferrite nanocomposites improve broadband absorption and bandwidth compared to pure hexaferrite.
Soft magnetic composite layers improved absorption by up to 40% in dB scale compared to the single MW layer.
Soft magnetic material layers increased absorption bandwidth more than soft magnetic composite layers.
Increasing the number of interfaces in composites enhances interfacial polarization, improving microwave absorption.
The bilayer approach allows continuous and controlled tuning of absorption frequency and bandwidth for stealth applications.
The weight filling factor of magnetic fillers in the composites was kept constant at 4%.
The total thickness of bilayer systems studied was submillimetric, typically below 1 mm.
The study used far-field radar conditions to simulate real radar detection environments.
